newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: War crimes trial hears witnesses via satellite.
newsitem.headline: War crimes trial hears witnesses via satellite.

text.p: The U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia began hearing evidence from witnesses via a satellite link from the Bosnian city of Banja Luka on Tuesday.
The tribunal has given lawyers defending Bosnian Serb Dusko Tadic special permission to call about 10 witnesses this week to testify on their client's behalf via the live satellite link.
Tadic is accused of killing, raping and torturing non-Serbs as part of an "ethnic cleansing" campaign in the Prijedor area of northwest Bosnia in 1992. He denies the charges.
Tadic's lawyers had asked for defence witnesses to be allowed to testify from Bosnia, saying some were unwilling or afraid to travel to The Hague for fear they might be arrested.
The judges ruled in June that because of the difficulties of conducting a trial relating to a recently ended conflict it was "in the interests of justice" to allow remote testimony.
They stressed this was an exception to the general rule that witnesses must testify in The Hague, adding that testimony via satellite would not weigh as heavily as evidence given in court.
The first satellite witness was a Serb called Zeljko Maric who said he had worked with Tadic as a traffic policeman in Tadic's home village of Kozarac and other places in the area.
Maric said Tadic had not expressed extreme Serb nationalist views and had condemned the war in Bosnia and the destruction of the largely Moslem village of Kozarac when it fell to the Serbs.
"Dusko condemned everything that was happening, including the war, and everything that was happening in our part of the world," he said through an interpreter.
Prosecution witnesses have testified that Tadic took an active role in rounding up his Moslem neighbours for deportation to prison camps where he and other Serbs maltreated them.
Maric was the twenty second defence witness to be called. Previous witnesses have included the defendant's wife Mira.
The Tadic trial is expected to finish in November and the judges are expected to deliver their verdict in the spring.
